lesson.title: Explicit Memory: Remembering on Purpose
lesson.summary: Explicit memory is the conscious, effortful recollection of facts and personal experiences, and it depends on medial temporal lobe structures like the hippocampus to bind scattered brain activity into a retrievable memory.
lesson.body:
You already know that the central nervous system is where information gets processed and stored, but not all storage works the same way. Explicit memory refers to the kind of remembering you can consciously bring to mind and describe in words ,  deliberately recalling something rather than just being unconsciously shaped by it. When you answer a test question, tell a friend what you did last weekend, or recite the boiling point of water, you are using explicit memory. Psychologists usually split it into two related types: episodic memory, which is your recollection of specific personal events tied to a time and place (what you ate for breakfast this morning), and semantic memory, which is your store of general facts and knowledge that isn't tied to when or where you learned it (knowing that Paris is the capital of France, even though you probably can't recall the exact moment you learned that).

The reason explicit memory behaves the way it does traces back to how the brain forms it. Encoding an explicit memory takes conscious attention ,  you have to actually notice and process information, often holding it briefly in working memory, before it can be stored for later use. That's why you can walk past hundreds of parked cars without remembering any of them, but you'll clearly remember the one that nearly hit you, because that event captured your focused attention. Once information is attended to, a brain structure in the medial temporal lobe called the hippocampus plays a central role in linking together the separate pieces of an experience ,  the sights, sounds, and context ,  that are actually processed in different regions of the cortex. Think of the hippocampus less like a filing cabinet holding the memory itself and more like an index card that tells the cortex how to reassemble a scattered set of details into one coherent memory when you try to recall it later.

This mechanism is exactly why damage to the hippocampus produces such a distinctive memory problem. In one of the most studied cases in psychology, a man known by his initials H.M. had large portions of his medial temporal lobes, including much of the hippocampus, surgically removed to control severe epileptic seizures. After the surgery, he could still hold a conversation, use language normally, and recall memories from long before the operation, but he was largely unable to form new explicit memories ,  he could meet the same person repeatedly and have no conscious recollection of ever meeting them before. His case, studied extensively over subsequent decades, helped convince researchers that explicit memory formation depends heavily on the hippocampus, while other kinds of learning can survive without it.

It's worth noticing what explicit memory is not, even without getting into the details of those other systems yet: it is specifically the remembering you can consciously access and report, tested by asking you to recall information freely or recognize it among options. When your psychology teacher gives you a multiple-choice question about a term from this chapter, they are testing your explicit memory ,  your ability to consciously retrieve a fact you deliberately encoded, connect it to the right context, and report it back on demand.
